# SK2061 — Both operands of the operator are the same expression

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

Both operands of `&&`, `||`, `&`, `|`, `^`, `-`, `/` or `%` are the same side-effect-free expression, so the operator answers a question about nothing.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S1764 |

## Why

`a && a`, `offset - offset`, `bits ^ bits` — one side was meant to name something else and a copy-paste left it naming the first. The result is a constant the compiler is happy to fold, and the check that was written to catch a case cannot catch it. ⚠ **The six comparison operators are not examined, and measuring rather than remembering is what settled that.** `csc` reports `q == q`, `q < q`, `this.g == this.g`, `b.v == b.v`, `Box.Which == Box.Which` and `a == a` on a string as `CS1718`, on by default; the only comparison shape it leaves silent is a property access, and `SK2012` already owns that. There was nothing left over, so the operators went. ⚠ **The rule must still know the operand's type, which is why it is semantic.** `x - x` on a `double` is a NaN-preserving zero, not a constant nothing.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (options.verbose || options.verbose) { Trace(); }
```

Write:

```csharp
if (options.verbose || options.diagnostics) { Trace(); }

// and the NaN-preserving zero, which is the same shape on a different type and is never reported:
var delta = x - x;
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The six comparison operators are not examined at all**, because `csc` already reports every shape this rule could have reported: `CS1718` covers simple names, `this.` paths, member access to a field, static fields, strings and reference equality, and it is on by default. The one comparison shape the compiler leaves silent is a property access, and `SK2012` already covers that with a proof about the accessor bodies this rule does not have. ⚠ **Doc 08's sentence that `CS1717`/`CS1718` "reach the identifier spellings only" is wrong and was refuted by this measurement** — it is true of properties, which is the example it was written from, and false of fields reached through a member access. ⚠ **Floating-point operands are excluded outright.** `x - x` on a `double` is 0 for every finite value and NaN for NaN and the infinities, which is a real technique for propagating NaN and is textually identical to the defect; `double`, `float`, `decimal` and their nullable forms never reach the report. ⚠ **Only side-effect-free paths of locals, parameters, fields, `this` and `base` are compared.** An invocation on either side is two evaluations that may differ — `reader.Read() - reader.Read()` is not a defect — and a property access is a method call whose two evaluations the rule does not attempt to prove equal. ⚠ **`Math.Max(x, x)` and `a.CompareTo(a)` are invocations, not operators, and are outside the subject entirely**; a generator emitting them is not reported. A user-defined operator, a lifted (nullable-operand) operation and an operand of an unresolved type are all excluded, because none of them has the meaning the rule assumes. `+`, `*`, `<<` and `>>` are not examined: doubling, squaring and shifting by oneself are ordinary arithmetic. `=` is not examined either — the compiler's own `CS1717` says it, and `SK2012` says the rest. Generated code is excluded.
